qs.q: In a child with eczema, allergic rhinitis and pollen‑induced wheeze, which immunoglobulin is central to the underlying allergic mechanism?
qs.e: IgE binds to FcεRI on mast cells and drives the allergic cascade. The other immunoglobulins are not primary mediators of atopic asthma.
qs.s: Asthma and the Lungs: Understanding How the Disease Affects: MCQs

qs.q: A 6‑year‑old with eczema and allergic rhinitis develops recurrent cough at night. Which underlying pathophysiological feature links these conditions?
qs.e: Eczema, allergic rhinitis, and asthma commonly share type 2 (T2) inflammation; the other options are not described as linking these atopic conditions.
qs.s: Childhood Asthma: Clinical Features, Diagnosis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A child with atopic dermatitis and allergic rhinitis develops nocturnal cough. Which cytokine most likely drives the airway inflammation?
qs.e: Interleukin‑5 promotes eosinophil maturation in type‑2 asthma; the other mediators are not central to this pathway.
qs.s: Childhood Asthma: Clinical Features, Diagnosis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 50-year-old male with a long-standing history of allergic rhinitis and asthma is evaluated for nasal congestion and bilateral nasal masses. Biopsy of the nasal polyps shows an oedematous stroma with a prominent eosinophilic infiltrate and thickened basement membrane, covered by ciliated columnar epithelium. This clinical presentation is part of which recognized syndrome?
qs.e: Samter's triad consists of asthma, nasal polyps, and aspirin sensitivity. The other syndromes involve entirely different organ systems and pathologies, such as autoimmune connective tissue disorders or paraneoplastic neurological findings.

qs.q: A child requires prophylactic treatment for perennial allergic rhinitis using nasal drops. Which agent acts exclusively as a mast cell stabilizer by inhibiting chloride channels and preventing histamine release?
qs.e: Cromolyn acts as a mast cell stabilizer by inhibiting chloride channels to prevent histamine release, functioning purely prophylactically. Beclomethasone is a corticosteroid that blocks phospholipase A2.

qs.q: A patient with allergic rhinitis is prescribed a medication that inhibits phospholipase A2, thereby decreasing arachidonic acid synthesis and reducing prostaglandins and leukotrienes. Which drug class is this?
qs.e: Corticosteroids act by blocking phospholipase A2, which suppresses arachidonic acid synthesis and downstream inflammatory mediators. Leukotriene receptor antagonists block specific leukotriene actions rather than inhibiting phospholipase A2.

qs.q: For daily prophylaxis of perennial allergic rhinitis in children, which drug class is most appropriate?
qs.e: Leukotriene receptor antagonists are given daily to prevent mast‑cell mediated rhinitis in children. Cromolyn is mainly for acute prophylaxis and steroids are reserved for more severe disease.

qs.q: A 24-year-old woman with moderate persistent allergic rhinitis experiences inadequate relief from oral antihistamines. Which intranasal anti-inflammatory agent is appropriate to add for first-line topical therapy?
qs.e: Intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone are the most effective first-line therapy for moderate persistent allergic rhinitis. Azelastine is an antihistamine spray, and ipratropium primarily targets rhinorrhea rather than the full inflammatory cascade.

ai.title: Allergic Rhinitis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Allergic rhinitis is an IgE‑mediated inflammation of the nasal mucosa triggered by common allergens. Diagnosis relies on history, physical exam and, where available, skin prick or specific IgE testing. Management focuses on avoidance, antihistamines and intranasal steroids.

sections.p: Allergic rhinitis is a type I hypersensitivity reaction of the nasal mucosa to inhaled allergens. It presents with sneezing, nasal congestion, rhinorrhoea and itchy eyes. Diagnosis is clinical; confirmatory tests are skin‑prick or serum specific IgE when available.
b: History of episodic symptoms linked to seasonal or perennial allergens
Physical exam: pale, boggy nasal mucosa, itchy conjunctiva

t.b: Identifies sensitisation to specific allergens – a wheal ≥3 mm larger than negative control confirms IgE‑mediated allergy
Quantifies IgE to particular allergens; useful when skin testing is contraindicated

sections.p: Severity is graded by the ARIA (Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma) system: intermittent vs persistent; mild vs moderate/severe. This guides treatment intensity.
b: Mild: symptoms do not interfere with daily activities
Moderate/severe: symptoms impair daily life or sleep

sections.p: In East Africa, perennial allergens such as dust mites, moulds, animal dander and pollens from grasses and trees are common. Infections (e.g., viral URIs) can trigger or exacerbate symptoms.
Patients report sneezing, nasal itching, rhinorrhoea, congestion and itchy, watery eyes. Symptoms are often worse at night or in the early morning and may be seasonal.
Routine investigations are usually unnecessary. Use tests only to rule out mimics or assess severity.

t.b: Rule out eosinophilia or infection; eosinophilia supports atopy but is not diagnostic
Exclude sinusitis, nasal polyps or asthma exacerbation if respiratory symptoms present
Assess for co‑existing asthma; normal in isolated rhinitis

sections.p: Red flags include sudden severe facial pain, purulent discharge, fever, visual changes or haemorrhage, suggesting sinusitis, orbital cellulitis or epistaxis. Complications can be chronic sinusitis, nasal polyps or asthma exacerbation.
Treat the trigger, provide symptomatic relief and monitor for complications. First‑line therapy is oral antihistamines; intranasal steroids are added for persistent or moderate/severe disease.
b: Avoidance: keep windows closed, use HEPA filters, wash bedding in hot water, remove pets
Oral antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine, loratadine) – rapid relief, minimal sedation

t.b: Reduces mucosal inflammation; first choice for persistent or moderate/severe disease – improves congestion and sneezing
Useful for mild intermittent symptoms when steroids are contraindicated
Long‑term disease modification in patients with clear sensitisation and persistent symptoms

sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 4–6 weeks of therapy. Reinforce avoidance measures and educate on correct inhaler use if asthma is co‑present.
Non‑allergic rhinitis (vasomotor, infectious, hormonal), sinusitis, nasal polyps and asthma.
b: Non‑allergic rhinitis – no IgE sensitisation, symptoms triggered by temperature or irritants

sections.p: Skin‑prick tests can be false‑negative in patients on antihistamines; specific IgE may be positive in asymptomatic atopic individuals.
b: Antihistamines suppress wheal response – discontinue 5 days before testing

faq.q: What if a patient has both dust mite and pollen allergy?
faq.a: Treat both; avoid dust mites year‑round and use pollen‑specific avoidance during peak seasons.

exam: What is the first line of treatment for moderate persistent allergic rhinitis? — Oral antihistamine plus intranasal steroid; explain why steroids are added.
A patient with nasal congestion and itchy eyes has a negative skin‑prick test. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Non‑allergic rhinitis; explain the difference in pathophysiology.
You are in a rural clinic with no access to steroids. What alternative therapy can you offer? — Oral antihistamine; discuss its limitations.
A child with allergic rhinitis also has wheeze. What additional investigation would you order? — Spirometry to assess for asthma.
Why is epinephrine avoided in treating allergic rhinitis? — It is for anaphylaxis, not for local nasal symptoms.
What is the ARIA classification for a patient with symptoms 5 days a week for 6 months? — Persistent moderate/severe; explain staging.
When should you refer a patient with allergic rhinitis to an allergist? — When symptoms are uncontrolled despite therapy or when immunotherapy is considered.
